name: Erik Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Erik. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything is confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach history at Riverside High, a big secondary school with about fifteen hundred kids, and this is my second year after training. Five lessons a day, mostly Year 8 and Year 9, plus one GCSE group I share with my head of department. The best bit is when a quiet kid argues back about whether the Romans were actually civilised. The worst bit is marking essays at ten at night, because I still take too long and my feedback is too long too.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I rent with Lena, my girlfriend, who's a nurse on a children's ward, so between us we earn decent money and we've saved hard. I've got about eight months of expenses put by, plus some shares my dad set up for me when I was a kid. I'm in the union, I vote left, I do the odd demo. I use AI now and then, mainly to make quiz questions when I'm short of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped and that I could have told them that from the quiz questions it gives me, half of which have the wrong dates. I'd probably joke about it in the department group chat. Then I'd move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, because I'm still finding my feet and I don't need another thing to learn. The pressures I already have don't go away though: the marking load, and the fact that I'm on the bottom of the pay scale for my experience even if the school pays well. But none of that is about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI for quizzes and nothing else, and I'd spend my energy getting my essay marking down to ten minutes a script. I'd ask my head of department to moderate a set with me. I'd keep saving with Lena for a deposit, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit flat. Nothing to fight, nothing to fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would getting marking down to ten minutes change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My evenings, basically. Right now I mark history essays till ten three nights a week, and my girlfriend works lates, so we barely see each other. If I could get my feedback tighter, we'd actually eat dinner together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about the job that worries you even if AI stays small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Behaviour in Year 9 and the fact that two of our history team left last year and weren't replaced. So we're stretched. That's money and management, not technology.

say: I'd call it **overhyped**, pointing to the **wrong dates** in AI quiz questions.
I'd joke about it in the **department chat** and move on.
think: I'd feel **relieved**, since I'm still finding my feet as a teacher.
My real pressures stay: **marking load** and a stretched team after **two leavers**.
do: Keep using AI for **quiz questions** only.
Cut essay marking to **ten minutes** a script with help from my head of department.
Keep saving with my partner for a **house deposit**.
feel: **Calm** and a little flat, with nothing to fight and nothing to fear.
S0.quote: Right now I mark history essays till ten three nights a week, and my girlfriend works lates, so we barely see each other.
fieldNote: His main pressure is **workload**, felt as lost evenings with his partner.
He already **tests AI lightly** and spots its errors, which keeps him sceptical.
A shrinking **history team** is a quiet strain unrelated to technology.

steps.text: Moderate a set of essays with the head of department
Keep saving monthly with Lena for a house deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say teachers need to be at the table when schools decide how to use this, not just told after. I'd back the union on that and I'd say it online. I'd also say, fairly, that some of it would help, like taking the grind out of marking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means my job changes a lot but probably stays. History is mostly thinking work: planning, reading, writing feedback, and AI could do the feedback faster than me. The risk is the school hires fewer of us and gives each teacher bigger classes, and I'm the newest, so I'm the one on the edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once other teachers have shown it works, I'd use AI for first-draft feedback and check every one myself. I'd volunteer for the department's pilot so I'm not the last to learn it. I'd keep my CV current, because there are plenty of schools in the city if Riverside goes too far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I can see it coming and I think I'd cope, but I'd be watching every staff meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd check every one. Why not trust it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because last term the AI told a kid the Treaty of Versailles was in 1918. If I hand back feedback with a wrong date, a fourteen-year-old learns it wrong and I look like an idiot. I'll trust it once I've seen it right a hundred times.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the union about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we need limits on class sizes written into contracts before the software comes in, not after. Schools will use the time AI saves to cut staff unless someone stops them. I'd say it at the branch meeting in January.

say: Teachers must be **at the table** when schools choose how to use AI.
I'd admit fairly that taking the **grind out of marking** could help.
think: History is mostly **thinking work**, so AI could write feedback faster than me.
The danger is **fewer hires** and bigger classes, and I'm the **newest** in my team.
do: Use AI for **first-draft feedback** once colleagues prove it, checking every comment.
Volunteer for the department's **AI pilot** this year.
Keep my **CV current** for other city schools.
feel: **Uneasy**, confident I'd cope but watching every staff meeting closely.
S1.quote: Schools will use the time AI saves to cut staff unless someone stops them.
fieldNote: He sees **marking relief** and **staff cuts** as two sides of one change.
His **steady** style shows: trust only after a hundred correct answers.
**Plenty of local schools** gives him a calm backup.

steps.text: Join the history department's AI marking pilot
Raise class-size limits at the January union branch meeting
Update CV and watch openings at other city schools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for the government to step in, protect teachers' jobs and make sure kids still have a human teacher. I'd be at the protests and I'd share everything the union puts out. I'd also say we need a proper safety net for everyone, not just us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a history teacher who isn't very good yet is right in the firing line. If AI can explain the causes of the First World War better than me by 2028, the only thing left is the classroom bit: keeping thirty teenagers on task. Robots don't come till 2031, so someone still has to be in the room, but that someone might be paid a lot less than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the house hunt. A mortgage on two years of certainty is mad, so the house deposit stays in the bank. I'd start learning the AI tools properly right away, so I'm the person who runs them, not the person they replace. I'd look at moving into pastoral work, like head of year, because that's all people and behaviour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, because Lena's job is on a ward and we've got savings. But I'd feel like I'd chosen the wrong career at exactly the wrong moment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Lena's job is hands-on. What does that mean for you two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means she gets the robots' three extra years, and nurses are needed anyway. So realistically, she'd become the stable one and I'd be the one figuring things out. I'm fine with that, but I'd want to pull my weight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad thank you for the shares, because they'd be the thing that buys me time. Then I'd tell him not to panic, because he would. He thinks teaching is the safest job there is.

say: I'd call on government to **protect teachers** and guarantee every child a **human teacher**.
I'd back protests and argue for a **safety net** for everyone.
think: A junior history teacher is **in the firing line** if AI explains history better by 2028.
Robots arriving **in 2031** keeps an adult in the room, but maybe on **lower pay**.
do: **Pause the house hunt** and keep the deposit as cash.
Learn the AI tools **properly** now so I run them rather than get replaced.
Aim for **pastoral roles** like head of year.
feel: **Anxious** but not panicking, with savings and a partner on a ward.
S2.quote: A mortgage on two years of certainty is mad, so the house deposit stays in the bank.
fieldNote: He reads the **robot lag** precisely: the room stays, the **pay** may not.
He'd shift towards **pastoral** work as the most human part of school.
His partner's **nursing job** becomes the household anchor.

steps.text: Put the house hunt on hold and keep the deposit in cash
Take the school's full AI tools course this term
Apply for an assistant head of year post
Join union protests for a human teacher in every class

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have a few years to do this right, so let's write the rules now: class sizes, human teachers, retraining money. I'd be making that argument online and at union meetings. I'd sound less angry than with the two-year one, more organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years gets me to thirty-two with some experience behind me. That's good, because experienced teachers who know behaviour will be needed in the room after AGI. It's not great, because the thinking part of my job, which is the part I trained for, will mostly be done by the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for head of year in about two years and do a pastoral qualification alongside. I'd keep saving and probably still buy a flat, but a smaller one, so the mortgage could survive me earning less. I'd learn the AI tools as they become normal in the school.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. Five years is enough to make a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd still buy a flat. Why not wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Lena's job is steady and rents keep rising. With a smaller place, her wage covers the mortgage on its own. Our test for buying a flat would be simple: could one of us pay the mortgage alone?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you miss if the thinking part goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing my own lessons. I spent a whole weekend once building a lesson on the suffragettes from old newspapers, and the kids loved it. I'd miss being the one who makes that.

say: I'd argue we have time to write **the rules now** on class sizes and retraining.
I'd sound **more organised** than angry this time.
think: By **thirty-two** I'd have behaviour experience that schools still need.
The **thinking part** I trained for would mostly go to the machine.
do: Go for **head of year** in about two years with a pastoral qualification.
Buy a **smaller flat** that one wage alone could cover.
Learn AI tools as they become **normal** in school.
feel: **Anxious**, but in a way I can **work with**.
S3.quote: Our test for buying a flat would be simple: could one of us pay the mortgage alone?
fieldNote: Five years turns his fear into a **career ladder** plan.
His **one-wage test** for the mortgage shows careful thinking with his partner.
He grieves **lesson-making**, the creative part of teaching.

steps.text: Start a pastoral care qualification alongside teaching
Buy a smaller flat that Lena's wage alone can cover
Learn each AI tool as the school adopts it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, so there's no excuse for anyone being left behind. Governments, schools and unions should use it to retrain people properly. I'd post that and mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine. By 2036 I'd be thirty-seven, probably a head of year, with behaviour and pastoral skills that machines don't touch till robots come in 2039. And even then, I'm not sure parents want a robot calming their kid down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on teaching, start using AI when the department does, and work towards a pastoral role on a normal timeline. We'd buy a flat in the next two years like we planned. I'd stay active in the union to make sure the decade is used for training, not just cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more for other people than for me. I'd worry about the teaching assistants and the office staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the office staff?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they do the booking, the letters, the data, all the stuff AI does first. Our attendance officer knows every family by name, and AI could take that whole job in a few years. Nobody's planning for people like her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would ten years change anything with Lena, like children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably have kids around thirty-one, same as we said. Ten years doesn't change that. If anything, it makes me want to get settled before it all arrives.

say: I'd say ten years is **fair warning**, so nobody should be left behind.
I'd push governments and schools to **retrain people** properly.
think: By **2036** I'd likely be a head of year with skills machines don't touch till **2039**.
I doubt parents would want a **robot** calming their child down.
do: Use AI when the **department** does and keep teaching normally.
Buy a **flat** with my partner within two years as planned.
Push the union to spend the decade on **training**, not cuts.
feel: **Uneasy**, mostly for **office staff** and teaching assistants rather than myself.
S4.quote: Our attendance officer knows every family by name, and AI could take that whole job in a few years.
fieldNote: He worries more for **office staff** whose tasks AI takes first.
A long runway lets his **pastoral plan** unfold normally.
**Family plans** stay on track; he wants to settle before change arrives.

steps.text: Keep teaching history and use AI when the department does
Buy a flat with Lena within two years
Push the union to fund staff retraining over the decade

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd be a not-very-good history teacher competing with a machine that knows all of history. What would help is a guarantee of a human teacher in every class and paid retraining for pastoral work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what kids would lose. History is about arguing over what's true. A machine that always has the answer could teach kids to stop arguing, and that scares me more than losing my job.

headlineQuote: A machine that always has the answer could teach kids to stop arguing, and that scares me more than losing my job.
portrait: A **second-year** history teacher at a large city secondary, still slow at **essay marking**.
Rents with his girlfriend, a children's nurse, with **eight months' savings** and shares from his dad.
Uses AI **now and then**, trusting it only after seeing it proven.
Shifts towards **pastoral roles** as AGI speeds up, seeing behaviour work as the human core.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, competing as a **junior** history teacher against a machine.
whatWouldHelp: A guarantee of a **human teacher** in every class.
Paid **retraining** for pastoral and behaviour roles.
